questions.problem: What is the domain in the $xy$-plane of the hyperbolic cylinder $\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{2}=1?$
questions.worked_solution:
The full expression describing all points on our hyperbolic cylinder is

$$
\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{2}=1,\,z=k
$$

where $k\in R$ can vary arbitrarily. 

The domain of any cylinder in the $xy$-plane is its base curve. Hence, in this case, the domain is

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\text{ }\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{2}=1}.
$$

This is a hyperbola centered at $(-1,4).$

questions.problem: What is the domain in the $xy$-plane of the elliptic cylinder $\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}=1?$
questions.worked_solution:
The full expression describing all points on our elliptic cylinder is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}=1,\,z=k
$$

where $k\in R$ can vary arbitrarily. 

The domain of any cylinder in the $xy$-plane is its base curve. Hence, in this case, the domain is

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{9}=1}
$$

which can be written as

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1}.
$$

This is an ellipse centered at $(0,3)$ with semi-axes of lengths $5$ and $3.$

questions.problem: The projection of the intersection between the hyperbolic cylinder $2(x+6)^{2}-5{y}^{2}=10$ and the plane $z=5$ onto the $xy$-plane is a hyperbola. What are the lengths of the semi-axes of the hyperbola?
questions.worked_solution:
To find the intersection of the cylinder and the plane $z=5,$ we substitute $z=5$ into the equation of the cylinder. However, since the equation has no (explicit) $z$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2(x+6)^{2}-5{y}^{2} & =10 \\ \frac{(x+6)^{2}}{5}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+6)^{2}}{(\sqrt{5})^{2}}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a hyperbola with semi-axes of lengths $\sqrt{5}$ and $\sqrt{2}.$

questions.problem: The projection of the intersection between the elliptic cylinder $9{x}^{2}+2(y-1)^{2}=18$ and the plane $z=1$ onto the $xy$-plane is an ellipse. What are the lengths of the semi-axes of the ellipse?
questions.worked_solution:
To find the intersection of the cylinder and the plane $z=1,$ we substitute $z=1$ into the equation of the cylinder. However, since the equation has no (explicit) $z$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}+2(y-1)^{2} & =18 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{(3)^{2}} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of an ellipse with semi-axes of lengths $\sqrt{2}$ and $3.$

questions.problem: What is the trace in the $xy$-plane of the elliptic cylinder $\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{4}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{6}=1?$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the trace in the $xy$-plane, we substitute $z=0$ into the equation of the cylinder, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(0)^{2}}{6} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-3)^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ (x-3)^{2} & =4 \\ x-3 & =\pm 2 \\ x & =3\pm 2 \\ x & =1,5\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of two lines $x=1$ and $x=5$ in the $xy$-plane.

questions.problem: What is the trace in the $yz$-plane of the parabolic cylinder $(x+3)^{2}=6y?$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the trace in the $yz$-plane, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the cylinder, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}(0+3)^{2} & =6y \\ 9 & =6y \\ y & =\frac{9}{6} \\ y & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a line in the $yz$-plane.

questions.problem: The projection of the intersection between the hyperbolic cylinder $3(x+1)^{2}-6(z-2)^{2}=12$ and the plane $y=1$ onto the $xz$-plane is a hyperbola. What are the lengths of the semi-axes of the hyperbola?
questions.worked_solution:
To find the intersection of the cylinder and the plane $y=1,$ we substitute $y=1$ into the equation of the cylinder. However, since the equation has no (explicit) $y$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3(x+1)^{2}-6(z-2)^{2} & =12 \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{(z-2)^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{(2)^{2}}-\frac{(z-2)^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a hyperbola with semi-axes of lengths $2$ and $\sqrt{2}.$

canonical_examples.problem: What is the domain in the $xy$-plane of the elliptic cylinder $\dfrac{x^2}{9} + (y+1)^2 = 1?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The full expression describing all points on our elliptic cylinder is

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{9} + (y+1)^2 = 1, \qquad z=k
$$

where $k \in \mathbb{R}$ can vary arbitrarily. 

The domain of any cylinder in the $xy$-plane is its base curve. Hence, in this case, the domain is

$$
\left\{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : \dfrac{x^2}{9} + (y+1)^2 = 1\right\}
$$

which can be written as

$$
\left\{ (x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : \dfrac{x^2}{3^2} + \dfrac{(y+1)^2}{1^2} = 1\right\}.
$$

This is an ellipse centered at $(0,-1)$ with semi-axes of lengths $3$ and $1.$

canonical_examples.problem: What is the trace in the $yz$-plane of the elliptic cylinder $\dfrac {x^2} 2 +  \dfrac {(y-2)^2}4  = 1?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the trace in the $yz$-plane, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the cylinder, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ (y-2)^{2} & =4 \\ y-2 & =\pm 2 \\ y & =2\pm 2 \\ y & =0,4\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of two lines $y=0$ and $y=4$ in the $yz$-plane.
